title: Amid official and uni discretion, Australia needs hubs that will critique China | The Strategist
paragraphs: Former West German chancellor Willy Brandt once said, ‘Foreign policy is too important to be left to governments alone.’ While governments must show leadership, foreign policy is a national endeavour in which civil society shares responsibility. This may have been less obvious during the Cold War, but it’s as clear as day in the current era of global competition and conflict in which distrust of government is a dominant feature.

Australia urgently needs to develop critical China hubs to play a role in informing society of the challenges China presents to the country and region. Called ‘critical’ because, unlike the government and universities, they would be unhindered in publicly critiquing the Chinese party-state, these hubs would play a supplementary role to official agencies. They’d publicly collect, analyse and disseminate information on China’s economic statecraft, United Front activities, educational influence, cyber and critical infrastructure challenges, regional aims and international influence operations.
Such hubs, bringing together China skills in the national interest, are already playing a positive role in other parts of the world.
